strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: controllable weather editing for autonomous driving, with an intrinsic-space formulation that aims to preserve scene geometry and material properties rather than editing pixels directly.

Proposes a two-component diffusion framework (weather-aware inverse renderer and weather-conditioned forward renderer) with novel components such as intrinsic map-aware attention (IMAA) and CLIP-space interpolation for fine-grained weather control.

Introduces two datasets, WeatherSynthetic (38k images) and WeatherReal (18k images), with intrinsic map annotations. These datasets, if released, would be a valuable resource for outdoor weather editing and intrinsic decomposition research.

Extensive experiments: comparisons with rendering-based methods, pixel-space editing methods, and weather restoration methods; quantitative and qualitative evaluations; user study; ablation studies; and downstream object detection/segmentation experiments.

Reports strong results in inverse rendering (over 10 dB PSNR improvement on several metrics) and competitive forward rendering results (best CLIP-S, second-best DINO-S among editing methods), with clear downstream gains on ACDC.
The paper discusses limitations, such as lack of temporal consistency for video and reliance on synthetic data, which is helpful for framing future work.
weaknesses: Some claims are overstated or not fully supported by the reported tables. For example, Table 1 shows Qwen-Image-Edit has higher average PickScore than the proposed method, and Table 3 shows DiffusionRenderer has better normal PSNR (28.68 vs. 25.06) and albedo LPIPS (0.34 vs. 0.35), contradicting statements that the method outperforms existing approaches across all evaluation metrics.

Comparison fairness is questionable. Several baselines (e.g., GeoWizard, IDArb, DiffusionRenderer) may not be fine-tuned on the proposed WeatherSynthetic dataset or designed for large-scale outdoor driving scenes, while the proposed method is trained on large-scale domain-specific synthetic data with ground-truth intrinsic maps. Prompt formats also differ between the proposed method and pixel-space editing baselines, making the reported margins less conclusive.

Method details are insufficient for reproducibility in the main paper. Key aspects are not specified: training objectives and losses, how the inverse renderer is trained on real data, how intrinsic maps are injected into the forward renderer, how weather-variant irradiance is handled during re-rendering, and details of the IMAA progressive training strategy. The paper repeatedly refers to supplementary material, leaving the main submission not self-contained.

The WeatherReal dataset is constructed using Flux-Kontext, a baseline method, to alter weather types, and pseudo-labels are generated by the inverse renderer. This introduces potential circularity and bias in the training/evaluation pipeline, and WeatherReal is not quantitatively evaluated for editing quality.

Downstream evaluation on ACDC shows improvements only for the proposed method; no comparison is provided against weather restoration or other editing baselines. The gains may reflect domain adaptation or hallucination rather than uniquely superior weather editing.

The CLIP-space interpolation for weather control lacks physical grounding and implementation details (e.g., choice of base prompt and relationship between alpha and weather intensity). It is demonstrated only qualitatively and may not guarantee physically plausible or consistent weather transitions.
Reproducibility is limited: code is not mentioned as released, datasets are not available at review time, and critical hyperparameters and training setups are absent from the main paper.

strengths: The paper proposes a physically motivated formulation for weather editing in intrinsic space, explicitly disentangling weather-variant illumination (irradiance) from weather-invariant material and geometry (albedo, roughness, metallicity, normal). This is a more interpretable and controllable alternative to pixel-space editing and is well motivated for autonomous driving.

The intrinsic map-aware attention (IMAA) mechanism is a sensible architectural contribution: it injects map-specific guidance into DiT attention via learnable map embeddings and gating, and the ablation in Table 3/Fig. 11 shows improved inverse-rendering quality and detail recovery compared with the no-IMAA variant.

The CLIP-space weather-direction interpolation provides a simple and effective mechanism for fine-grained weather intensity control, as demonstrated qualitatively in Fig. 7, and leverages the Stable Diffusion prior through feature distillation.

The paper constructs and plans to release two datasets, WeatherSynthetic (38K) and WeatherReal (18K), with intrinsic-map annotations. This addresses a real gap in outdoor/autonomous-driving intrinsic decomposition and weather-editing data.

The experimental section is broad: it compares against pixel-space editing methods, weather-restoration methods, and rendering-based methods, and includes downstream evaluations on ACDC where detection AP75 improves from 13.15 to 24.60 and segmentation mIOU from 24.13 to 30.05. The user study also reports 81.67% preference for the proposed method.

The inverse-rendering results in Table 3 are strong across albedo, normal, roughness, metallicity, and irradiance, and the qualitative comparisons in Figs. 6, 9, and 10 illustrate cleaner geometry preservation and more plausible weather removal/synthesis than several baselines.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the framework heavily relies on existing components (Stable Diffusion 3.5, DINOv2, CLIP prompt interpolation, intrinsic decomposition ideas from RGB↔X/DiffusionRenderer), while the main new module, IMAA, is an attention-bias/gating mechanism whose training schedule, losses, and feature-distillation details are largely deferred to the supplementary material.

Baseline comparisons may not be fully fair. In Table 3, IID and RGB↔X are fine-tuned on WeatherSynthetic, but other inverse-rendering baselines such as GeoWizard, IDArb, and DiffusionRenderer appear to be evaluated without equivalent weather/outdoor adaptation. The enormous PSNR margins (e.g., albedo 27.99 vs. 11.91) likely reflect a dataset/protocol mismatch rather than a fully controlled method comparison.

For forward rendering, the proposed method does not dominate all reported metrics: Qwen-Image-Edit achieves higher PickScore across all weather types, and Flux-Kontext achieves higher DINO-S. The paper acknowledges these results but relies on CLIP-S and qualitative arguments to claim superiority, making the evidence for forward-rendering quality less conclusive.

Quantitative real-world evaluation is limited. WeatherReal is used only for finetuning and is explicitly not used for evaluation, while real-world inverse-rendering and forward-rendering results are qualitative (Figs. 9 and 10). Claims about generalization to real-world adverse weather are therefore not fully substantiated quantitatively.

The WeatherReal dataset is built using pseudo-labels from the paper’s own inverse renderer and Flux-Kontext, followed by manual checking. This introduces potential circularity and bias in the training data; details about the manual checking protocol, acceptance rate, and pseudo-label noise are missing from the main paper.

Reproducibility is only partially supported. The datasets are promised but not yet released, and the main paper omits key implementation details such as exact network architecture, training hyperparameters, loss weights, and the IMAA progressive-training heuristic, which are needed to reproduce the results.

The paper acknowledges that the framework is single-image and not temporally consistent for video (Fig. 12). While this is honestly discussed as a limitation, temporal consistency is important for many weather-editing applications, and the current method does not address it.

strengths: The problem is relevant and well motivated: controllable weather editing for autonomous driving is a real need, and the intrinsic-space formulation (decompose into weather-invariant material/geometry plus weather-variant irradiance, then re-render) is a sensible way to gain controllability over pixel-space editing.

The paper is reasonably broad in its empirical effort: quantitative comparisons (PickScore/CLIP-S/DINO-S, PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), qualitative comparisons against Flux-Kontext, Qwen-Image-Edit, WeatherWeaver and Instruct-Pix2Pix, a 61-participant user study, downstream detection/segmentation experiments, and ablations on IMAA and WeatherReal.

Two new datasets are constructed (WeatherSynthetic, 38k images with UE5-rendered ground-truth intrinsic maps; WeatherReal, 18k real driving images), which if released would be a useful resource for weather-diverse outdoor inverse/forward rendering.

Several results are qualitatively convincing: Fig. 6 and Fig. 8 suggest the method better preserves scene geometry/material (e.g., removing snow accumulation and restoring lighting) than pixel-space and restoration baselines, and Fig. 7 illustrates plausible fine-grained weather transitions via CLIP-space interpolation.

The intrinsic map-aware attention (IMAA) idea — gating DINOv2 patch tokens with per-map learnable embeddings to bias DiT attention — is a plausible and reasonably simple mechanism, and the ablation in Table 3/Fig. 11(a) indicates it helps decomposition.
weaknesses: The headline quantitative claim is not credible as presented. In Table 3 the fine-tuned RGB<->X baseline reaches only 11.59 dB PSNR on albedo while the proposed method reaches 27.99 dB; IID (w/ finetune) gets 11.55 dB. A model that has been fine-tuned on the target dataset should not produce near-noise-level PSNR, which strongly suggests a color-space/normalization mismatch (the paper notes images are 'in linear space without tone mapping') or an unfair training budget ('the same training steps' is never defined). Since PSNR on linear/HDR intrinsic maps is itself a questionable metric, the abstract's 'over 10 dB PSNR improvement' — and the corresponding conclusion that the method 'outperforms state-of-the-art' inverse rendering — is unsupported until the evaluation protocol is clarified.

The downstream-task evidence (Table 2) does not support the claimed superiority. It only reports DETR/Segformer before vs. after applying the authors' own editing (AP75 13.15 -> 24.60, mIOU 24.13 -> 30.05). No competing editing/restoration method is run through the same downstream pipeline, so the table only shows the well-known fact that de-weathering helps perception, not that WeatherDiffusion is better for downstream tasks than AWRaCLe/Histoformer/WeatherWeaver.

The main text omits nearly all methodological substance. There is no training objective/loss for either the inverse or forward renderer, no architecture or hyperparameter details, no description of the feature distillation from Stable Diffusion 3.5, and the 'heuristic-guided progressive training strategy' for IMAA is explicitly deferred to the supplementary. For a method paper this is a serious clarity and reproducibility gap; the datasets are also only promised ('will be released') and cannot be inspected.

Self-referential data construction undermines several claims. WeatherReal's 'intrinsic map annotations' are pseudo-labels produced by the authors' own inverse renderer ('We use our inverse renderer to generate intrinsic maps ... of Waymo and KITTI'), and its weather variants are generated by Flux-Kontext — which is then used as a competing baseline. The abstract's statement that both datasets come 'with intrinsic map annotations' overstates the real-world dataset, and training the forward renderer on Flux-Kontext outputs while claiming to beat Flux-Kontext is circular.

Metric interpretation is selective and internally inconsistent. The introduction claims 'better DINO-based structural alignment,' yet Table 1 shows Ours 73.63 vs. Flux-Kontext 85.50 on DINO-S; DINO-S is dismissed as not measuring 'physical consistency and editing plausibility' only where the method loses. Similarly, on PickScore the method wins only the Foggy column (Sunny: Qwen 20.77 > Flux 20.72 > Ours 20.59; Rainy: Qwen 21.56 > Ours 20.76), but the text singles out Qwen as having 'a slightly higher PickScore,' omitting Flux's Sunny advantage, and converts a 0.52 CLIP-S margin into the claim of 'the most text-aligned and plausible' results.

There is a conceptual tension that is never analyzed: albedo, roughness, normal and metallicity are asserted to be weather-invariant, yet rain films and snow accumulation demonstrably alter surface albedo/roughness and geometry. The decomposition is under-constrained, and the paper provides no analysis or metric showing that the model attributes accumulation to weather rather than baking it into the 'invariant' material maps (or vice versa).

Novelty is moderate and the comparison set is incomplete. The framework largely recombines existing components — diffusion-based intrinsic decomposition (RGB<->X, DiffusionRenderer), CLIP embedding arithmetic for editing, attention bias/gating for control — and the forward renderer is distilled from Stable Diffusion 3.5. Relevant weather-editing/restoration methods discussed in related work (WeatherEdit, ClimateNeRF, WeatherGAN, ColorPix2Pix, TransWeather) are never compared, and weather-restoration baselines are compared only qualitatively (Fig. 8).

Weather-editing quality is evaluated only through proxy metrics (PickScore, CLIP-S, DINO-S) and a user study whose setup and results are relegated to the supplementary; there is no distributional metric (e.g., FID/KID) or material/geometry-consistency metric, and margins over the strongest baselines are within noise (~0.2-0.5 PickScore).

strengths: The paper addresses controllable weather editing by moving from pixel-space manipulation to intrinsic-space decomposition, disentangling material/geometry/illumination and enabling fine-grained weather prompts via CLIP-space direction interpolation.

It introduces an intrinsic map-aware attention (IMAA) mechanism with DINOv2-based patch gating and learned per-map embeddings; ablations show IMAA improves inverse-rendering quality across albedo, normal, roughness, metallic, and irradiance maps.

Two datasets, WeatherSynthetic and WeatherReal, are constructed with intrinsic map annotations and diverse weather/driving scenarios; this is a useful resource for outdoor weather editing and autonomous driving robustness research.

The experimental suite is extensive: comparisons against rendering-based methods, pixel-space editing methods, and weather restoration methods; user study; downstream evaluation on ACDC showing improvements such as DETR AP75 from 13.15 to 24.60 and Segformer mIOU from 24.13 to 30.05.
The supplementary material provides useful implementation details, training schedules, architecture of IMAA, feature distillation, and additional ablations, which improves transparency.
Limitations are discussed candidly, including single-image focus, lack of temporal consistency for video, and failure cases under dense fog.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the method combines existing components such as Stable Diffusion 3.5, DINOv2, flow matching, LoRA, and CLIP interpolation, while intrinsic decomposition with diffusion has already been explored in works like RGB<->X and DiffusionRenderer.

Inverse-rendering comparisons may be uneven: IID and RGB<->X are fine-tuned on WeatherSynthetic, but DiffusionRenderer, GeoWizard, and IDArb are not fine-tuned for outdoor weather conditions, making the very large reported margins (e.g., albedo PSNR 27.99 vs. 11.91) potentially reflect baseline mismatch rather than purely method superiority.

Forward-rendering results are mixed: the method achieves the best CLIP-S but is below Flux-Kontext on DINO-S and below Qwen-Image-Edit on PickScore across several weather conditions (e.g., rainy 20.76 vs. 21.56), so the claim of overall superiority should be more carefully qualified.

WeatherReal annotations are generated as pseudo-labels by the inverse renderer trained on synthetic data and Flux-Kontext, which may introduce confirmation bias and limit the independence of real-world validation.

The downstream detection/segmentation gains may be partly due to illumination or contrast normalization rather than improved weather understanding; no control experiment or statistical significance test is provided to isolate the effect.

Some dataset details are inconsistent or insufficiently specified: the main text mentions 38k synthetic images while the supplementary table reports 35k, and code release is not clearly promised, which affects reproducibility.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated intrinsic-space formulation for controllable weather editing, decomposing scenes into weather-invariant material/geometry and weather-variant irradiance, which is a novel and useful direction beyond pixel-space editing.

Proposes intrinsic map-aware attention (IMAA) with gating based on DINOv2 patch tokens and map embeddings; ablation in Tab. 2/Fig. 11 shows it improves decomposition (e.g., albedo PSNR 27.99 vs 26.78, normal 25.06 vs 23.63) and helps recover fine geometry.

CLIP-space weather-direction interpolation provides fine-grained controllable weather synthesis, and Fig. 7 qualitatively demonstrates smooth transitions (e.g., Intensity=0.3 to 1.0) compared with WeatherWeaver's blending-like results.

Strong empirical effort: two new datasets (WeatherSynthetic 38k, WeatherReal 18k), quantitative inverse-rendering comparisons (Tab. 3), forward-rendering comparisons (Tab. 1), user study (81.67% preference), and downstream detection/segmentation gains (Tab. 2: AP75 +11.45, mIOU +5.92 on ACDC), which together support practical utility.
Paper is generally clear, with a detailed supplementary covering implementation, dataset construction, additional ablations, and failure cases, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Forward-rendering evaluation relies heavily on CLIP/DINO/PickScore and a user study; while suitable for generative editing, there is limited quantitative assessment of physical fidelity (e.g., photometric/geometric consistency) for synthesized weather images beyond downstream tasks.

WeatherReal annotations are pseudo-labels produced by the authors' inverse renderer and only manually checked; this introduces possible circularity, and the quality of real-world intrinsic map supervision is not quantitatively validated.

Some baseline comparisons may not be fully apples-to-apples: indoor-focused methods (IID, RGB↔X) are fine-tuned for their setting, and DiffuserRenderer is adapted to outdoor driving scenes, which could affect the magnitude of reported inverse-rendering gains (e.g., albedo PSNR 27.99 vs 11.91).

Temporal consistency is not addressed; the paper acknowledges single-image editing and Fig. 12/failure cases show limitations for video or extreme weather, which is a meaningful gap for autonomous driving applications.

The pipeline depends on multiple large pre-trained models (Stable Diffusion 3.5, DINOv2, Qwen2.5-VL) and substantial compute (e.g., 40 hours on 7 L40S GPUs for forward renderer), and the datasets/models are not yet released, which may hinder reproducibility and adoption.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem: controllable weather editing for autonomous driving and robust perception under adverse weather.

Proposes a substantial framework that combines diffusion-based inverse rendering and forward rendering in intrinsic space, with weather-invariant material/geometry maps and weather-variant irradiance.
Introduces intrinsic map-aware attention (IMAA) to improve spatial correspondence and decomposition quality, supported by ablations and qualitative comparisons.

Constructs two new datasets, WeatherSynthetic and WeatherReal, which could be useful resources for weather editing and intrinsic decomposition in outdoor driving scenes, although the real-world intrinsic maps are pseudo-labeled.

Reports extensive experiments: comparisons with pixel-space editing methods, weather restoration methods, and inverse rendering baselines; ablations on IMAA, WeatherReal, and feature distillation; user study; and downstream detection/segmentation evaluation.
The paper is generally well organized and includes a detailed supplementary material with implementation and dataset construction details.
weaknesses: The central claim that intrinsic-space editing is superior to pixel-space editing is not directly validated with a controlled experiment: there is no comparison against a pixel-space variant using the same diffusion backbone and training data, so the source of the improvement is ambiguous.

The downstream evaluation in Table 2 is insufficient: it only compares DETR/Segformer with and without the proposed editing, not against baseline weather editing methods, and the protocol is unclear (e.g., test-time augmentation vs. replacement). Gains may simply come from converting adverse-weather images to sunny images, not from the proposed method specifically.

Inverse rendering on real-world data relies on pseudo-labels generated by the same inverse renderer used in training/fine-tuning, creating a circular evaluation risk. The manual quality check is not systematic and no quantitative validation of pseudo-label quality is provided.

There are inconsistencies in dataset sizes and annotations, e.g., the abstract reports 38K images while the supplementary reports 35K; the ground-truth status of WeatherReal intrinsic maps is unclear despite table checkmarks.

The main editing comparison shows PickScore lower than Qwen-Image-Edit and Flux-Kontext across multiple weather conditions. The state-of-the-art claim therefore rests mainly on CLIP-S, DINO-S, and a relatively small user study (61 participants) without statistical significance or confidence intervals.

Several baselines (e.g., IID, RGB↔X, GeoWizard, IDArb) are designed for indoor or different settings, and not all are fine-tuned equally, making comparison fairness questionable. The domain gap may inflate the reported margins.

Reproducibility is limited: the method depends on large pretrained/proprietary models (Stable Diffusion 3.5, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct) and pseudo-labels, with no clear statement that code or full annotations will be released.
Failure cases and limitations (e.g., hallucination under dense fog, temporal inconsistency) are largely deferred to the supplementary material, while the main text overstates robustness.
